splash.label: Animation: the message ATTACK AT DAWN is encrypted six times, once per era: with Caesar's wheel, with Vigenère's keyword, with an Enigma machine, with AES, with a public key, and hidden in a lattice.

cap.caesar: c. 50 BC · Caesar shifts every letter three places along the alphabet. There are only 25 keys: try them all.
cap.vigenere: 1553 · Bellaso (credited to Vigenère) shifts each letter by a letter of a keyword. “Indecipherable” for 300 years, until Babbage and Kasiski.
cap.enigma: 1918–1945 · Enigma: three rotors step with every key press, so the same letter never encrypts the same way twice. Broken by Rejewski and Turing.
cap.aes: 2001 · AES: the letters become 16 bytes and go through ten rounds of substitution, shifting, mixing and key. Still unbroken.
cap.publickey: 1976–77 · Diffie, Hellman, Rivest, Shamir and Adleman: Bob publishes an open padlock; anyone can lock with it, only Bob can open.
cap.lattice: 2024 · After Shor: a secret hidden as a lattice point plus noise. Easy with the right key, hard even for a quantum computer (ML-KEM).

cl.freqLabel: Letter frequencies of the ciphertext (dark bars) over those of English (light bars).
cl.long: Cryptography is the art of writing so that only the intended reader can understand. For most of history it was a craft of priests, diplomats and soldiers, and every cipher that was used widely was eventually broken. The breakers were patient people who counted letters, looked for repeated words and guessed what a message was likely to say. A cipher that hides the frequencies of the letters, that never repeats itself, and whose key is as long as the message is safe even against them; but such a cipher is hard to use. The history of the subject is the story of that trade off between security and convenience, told by the people who designed the systems and by the people who broke them. Today the same story continues with computers, with mathematics instead of pencils, and with new threats such as quantum machines on the horizon.

bk.feistelNote: F is not invertible (F({a}) = F({b}) = {y} with the first round key), yet the network is: the ciphertext {c} decrypts back with the same F and the keys in reverse.
bk.need16: Both plaintext and key must be exactly 16 bytes (32 hex digits).

op.input: The 16 bytes of the block fill a 4×4 grid column by column: the state.
op.addRoundKey: AddRoundKey: every byte is XORed with a byte of the round key. The only step that uses the key.
op.subBytes: SubBytes: every byte is replaced through the S-box (inversion in GF(2⁸) plus an affine map). This is the non-linear part: confusion.
op.shiftRows: ShiftRows: row r rotates r places to the left, so each column now mixes bytes from four different columns.
op.mixColumns: MixColumns: each column is multiplied by a fixed matrix over GF(2⁸): every output byte depends on all four input bytes. Diffusion.

pk.dhLabel: Diagram: public colour and numbers in the middle, each side mixes in its secret; both end with the same shared colour and number.
pk.eve: Eve sees p = {p}, g = 5, A = {A} and B = {B}. To get the secret she must find a from A = 5ᵃ mod p: a discrete logarithm.
pk.samePrime: p and q must be different primes.
pk.badE: e must have no common factor with φ(n) = {phi}: choose another e.
pk.squareMultiply: Decrypting {m}: d = {d} = {bits} in binary, so square-and-multiply takes {steps} squarings and {mults} multiplications instead of d − 1 multiplications.
pk.cracked: n = {n} = {p} × {q}, found by trial division in {ms} ms. From p and q the attacker computes d = {d}. Real RSA uses primes of over 1,500 bits.

cv.realLabel: The curve over the real numbers with points P and Q, the line through them, its third intersection and its reflection P+Q.
cv.infinity: P and Q are opposite: the line is vertical and P + Q = O, the point at infinity.
cv.finiteLabel: All the points of y² = x³ + 2x + 3 modulo 97, and the multiples of G.
cv.readout: {k}·G = ({x}, {y}). G has order {n}; the curve has {count} points counting O. Given only ({x}, {y}), finding {k} is the discrete logarithm problem.

pq.latticeLabel: A two-dimensional lattice, its basis vectors and a target point; click to move the target.
pq.found: Rounding with this basis lands on the closest lattice point (distance {d}). Click anywhere to move the target.
pq.missed: Rounding with this basis lands at distance {d}, but the closest point is at {best}. Same lattice, useless basis: that is the public key.
pq.lweLabel: Each encrypted bit as a point on a circle of q values: near 0 it decrypts to 0, near q/2 to 1. Noise spreads the points.
pq.tooNoisy: Too much noise: the sum of the errors crosses q/4 and some bits flip. Real schemes choose parameters so this almost never happens.
pq.allGood: Every bit decrypts: the noise is small enough. Without the secret s, the noise makes the public key look random.
